lines: Quantum mechanics predicts
what an instrument will read
with extraordinary precision,
and what that arithmetic describes
has been argued for a hundred years.
Each interpretation is a working scaffold
inside its own range.
A map drawn over all of them,
to reconcile them from above,
repeats the difficulty it set out to end.
Every measurement is taken by someone,
at some point along a chain.
That point is the cut.
The cut moves, and it never vanishes;
where a theory tries to erase it or fix it
in place is where the theory stops
being universal.
Faced with the standoff, a familiar move
is to imagine a higher space and lay
the interpretations out in it as regions.
The axes are things like process,
implicate order,
wholeness and self-reference.
The older pictures land in a mechanical,
local corner, and the newer ones
are placed toward process and the whole.
With every tension turned
into a direction,
the schools look settled,
each with an address on one tidy sheet.
Each of these is a tool that works
where it was made to work.
Copenhagen keeps a laboratory disciplined:
the quantum state on one side,
the classical pointer on the other.
Many worlds keeps the evolution whole,
which suits quantum information
and computing.
Bohm's mechanics
gives the particle a trajectory again.
The Bayesian and relational readings show
that a state is held by someone,
in a situation.
The computational pictures open
a new geometry to explore.
Inside its own boundary,
each one does real work.
Sorting ideas is not the same
as extending what is known.
The standard theory describes
identical electrons by a state
that changes sign when two are exchanged,
and Pauli's exclusion follows from that.
Restate it as a constraint on unfolding,
or as an undivided pattern,
and the equation predicts exactly
what it did.
A careful map says so itself,
and marks the sign as an open problem.
Call the correlations
in Bell's experiments
one process folded into itself,
and the statistics stay the same.
A map shows which concepts are neighbours.
Taking the sorting for an answer steps
past what the map can do.
Under the dispute is a line
that von Neumann and Heisenberg drew.
A system evolving
as a sum of possibilities has to meet,
somewhere, an instrument
that gives one definite record.
That meeting place is the measurement cut.
Von Neumann showed it can be moved:
between the particle and the screen,
between the screen and the retina,
between the optic nerve and the cortex.
However far back
along the chain it is pushed,
the calculated probabilities
do not change at all.
The cut slides freely,
and it cannot be taken out.
The habit is to search
the world of objects
for the place where collapse happens.
But along the chain, the particle,
the detector, the light
in the eye and the current in the nerve
can all be written as one evolving sum.
Nothing in that description
is marked: here.
To say the cut is at the screen
means the experimenter has decided
to stop tracking possibilities there
and to take what happened
as a readable fact.
Bohr made the same point:
there is no quantum object apart
from the arrangement set up to meet it,
and the arrangement
is a question someone chose to ask.
This is not a fiction of the mind.
It is how the one who asks is anchored.
The cut is a seam with two sides.
Where to cut and how is chosen:
position or momentum,
detectors behind the slits or none,
read the screen now or carry
the instrument further into the sum.
What comes back at the cut is not chosen:
the readings follow the Born rule,
whatever is wished.
And each reading, the moment it registers,
is already an effect,
and at once a cause of what follows.
Whatever is read has already happened,
so the cause is always at least
one step ahead of the record.
Seen in time, the cut is that gap.
Seen this way,
two old efforts come into view.
Objective collapse theories look in nature
for a constant or a threshold
that would make the cut a thing.
The strongest form
of many worlds removes it,
and then cannot say why one reading,
and only one, is met.
Both treat the edge of a first-person act
as a prop on a third-person stage.
The schools differ in where they place
the cut: at the apparatus,
in the branch, in a hidden trajectory,
in an updated belief, in a bounded sample.
It moves because the asker chooses
where along the chain to meet resistance.
It cannot be removed
because the first person
comes before any account:
even an account that leaves
the asker out is given by someone.
The same holds outside physics.
Shrink a language model weight
by weight, down to noise:
nothing in the numbers marks the size
at which a mind would be gone,
and whoever names one has drawn the line.
On the map,
self-reference is one more axis.
A theory that writes the observer
into its loop scores high;
one that leaves the observer
outside the experiment scores low.
The best of such maps note
that the loop never fully closes.
But a score is given from outside,
and self-reference is not an exhibit
that can be set on a table and graded.
It is the mind's unceasing differentiation
from itself.
The gaze that examines cannot be turned
into one of the specimens it examines.
Gödel, Tarski and Turing
showed the formal side of this:
a system that tries to describe a whole
that includes itself
cannot close from the inside.
From that comes a second,
quieter view from nowhere.
The mapmaker compares Copenhagen,
many worlds
and the hidden-variable schools
from above, and at the summit observer
and flow are one.
A careful map admits that its summit
is partly its own construction.
One question is still open:
where is the mapmaker standing?
Every school is read off a single graph,
and to spread them flat on that grid,
the one drawing has to assume
a place outside every branch,
bound by no cut at all.
The map faults classical physics
for its God's eye,
and takes a seat one level higher.
This is also
why language models turn out such maps
so readily.
A model folds what people
have written into one smooth space,
where hypotheses that contradict
each other become neighbouring clusters,
and self-reference and process
are easy tags to attach.
The model itself stands at no bench.
No irreversible measurement
has ever cost it anything.
A view that claims no source
has left out the embodied contact
that every physical regularity
was first read from.
Wanting a final theory comes from taking
the scaffold for a closed whole.
Every model,
from wave mechanics to the process maps,
is an instrument made for contact
with what has not been modelled yet.
It is not a shelter
where the asking can be set down.
However far the cut is pushed,
the Born weights hold.
If some link
in the chain produced the one result,
moving the cut past that link
would change something,
and nothing changes; so definiteness
is asserted at the boundary,
by whoever takes the reading as settled,
and is not produced
by the machinery before it.
To say the cut moves and never vanishes
takes nothing from physics.
It marks how far each model reaches.
With the seat at nowhere given up,
the next step leaves the finished map
for the open world.
The cut moves, and it never vanishes.
